en: Itivuttaka 110 Catukkanipāta Brāhmaṇadhammayāgavagga Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” they replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of gifts. What four? The gift of material things, the gift of Dhamma, the gift of safety, and the gift of loving-kindness. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of gifts. When this was said, a certain brahmin approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him. When they had concluded their greetings and cordial talk, he sat down to one side and said to the Blessed One: “Master Gotama, what is the difference between one who offers a sacrifice and one who enjoys the fruit of that sacrifice? “Brahmin, if one offers a sacrifice without having first made an offering, one is called a ‘sacrificer,’ while one who enjoys the fruit of that sacrifice is called an ‘enjoyer. But if one offers a sacrifice after having first made an offering, one is called a ‘sacrificer,’ and one who enjoys the fruit of that sacrifice is called a ‘partaker. [The brahmin asked: “And how, Master Gotama, does one offer a sacrifice after having first made an offering? “Here, brahmin, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. “Having thus offered an offering to the Triple Gem, he gives a gift to those ascetics and brahmins who refrain from taking life, from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, and from fermented liquor, wine, and intoxicants, which are the basis for negligence. This is how, brahmin, one offers a sacrifice after having first made an offering. “Now, brahmin, as to the difference between one who offers a sacrifice and one who enjoys the fruit of that sacrifice: if one offers a sacrifice without having first made an offering, one is called a ‘sacrificer,’ while one who enjoys the fruit of that sacrifice is called an ‘enjoyer. But if one offers a sacrifice after having first made an offering, one is called a ‘sacrificer,’ and one who enjoys the fruit of that sacrifice is called a ‘partaker. [The brahmin said: “Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama!... From today let Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life. [The Blessed One said: “Brahmin, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who sacrifices for himself but not for others; the person who sacrifices for others but not for himself; the person who sacrifices neither for himself nor for others; and the person who sacrifices both for himself and for others. These, brahmin, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. [The brahmin said: “Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama!... Just as one might set upright what was overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, even so has Master Gotama demonstrated the Dhamma in many ways. I go to Master Gotama for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life. The Carasutta:
Thus it was said by the Blessed One, so I have heard:
"Monks, even if sensual thought, ill-will thought, or harmful thought should arise in a monk while he is walking..."
If, monks, a bhikkhu tolerates that [thought], does not abandon it, does not dispel it, does not bring it to an end, and does not cause it to cease,
then even while walking, such a bhikkhu— being without ardor and without self-reproach, constantly and continuously lazy— is called one of inferior energy.
And if, monks, when a bhikkhu is standing, a thought of sensual desire, a thought of ill will, or a thought of cruelty arises...
If, monks, a bhikkhu tolerates that [thought], does not abandon it, does not dispel it, does not bring it to an end,

and does not cause it to cease, then even while standing, monks, such a bhikkhu— being without ardor, without fear of wrongdoing, constantly and continuously lazy, and of inferior energy— is called one who is indolent.
And if, monks, when a bhikkhu is sitting, there arises in him a thought of sensual desire, or a thought of ill will, or a thought of cruelty...
If, monks, a monk tolerates that [thought], does not abandon it, does not dispel it, does not bring it to an end,
and does not cause it to vanish, then even while sitting, such a monk is called one who is without ardor, without self-reproach, constantly and continuously lazy,
and of inferior energy. And if, monks, while a monk is lying down and awake, there arises in him a thought of sensual desire, or a thought of ill will, or a thought of cruelty...
If, monks, a bhikkhu tolerates that [thought], does not abandon it, does not dispel it, does not bring it to an end, and does not cause it to cease, then even while lying down, monks,
such a bhikkhu who is awake is called one who is without ardor, without fear of wrongdoing, constantly and continuously lazy,
and of inferior energy. And if, monks, sensual thought, ill will, or harmful thought arises in a bhikkhu even while he is walking...
If, monks, a bhikkhu does not tolerate that, but abandons it, dispels it, brings it to an end, and makes it non-existent;
then, monks, even while walking, such a bhikkhu is called “ardent, ashamed, constantly and continuously energetic, and resolute.
And if, monks, while a bhikkhu is standing, there arises in him a thought of sensual desire, or a thought of ill will, or a thought of cruelty...
If, monks, a bhikkhu does not tolerate that, but abandons it, dispels it, brings it to an end, and causes it to cease,
then even while standing, monks, such a bhikkhu— one who is ardent, possessed of a sense of shame, constantly and continuously energetic, and resolute—
is called one who has exerted himself. And if, monks, when a bhikkhu is sitting, a thought of sensual desire, a thought of ill will, or a thought of cruelty arises...
If, monks, a monk does not tolerate that [thought], but abandons it, dispels it, brings it to an end, and causes it to cease,
then even while sitting, monks, such a monk is called ardent, possessed of moral dread, constantly and continuously energetic,
and resolute. And if, monks, while a monk is lying down and awake, there arises in him a thought of sensual desire, a thought of ill will, or a thought of cruelty...
“If, monks, a monk does not tolerate that [thought], but abandons it, dispels it, brings it to an end, and causes it to cease,
then even while lying down, monks, a monk who is thus awake— one who is ardent, possessed of a sense of shame, constantly and continuously energetic, and resolute— is called such.
Thus the Blessed One spoke this matter.
In this regard, it is said:
Whether walking or standing,
sitting or lying down;
Whoever applies a thought that is evil and based on the household life has entered upon a wrong path.
One who is infatuated with things that cause delusion—
such a bhikkhu is incapable of touching the supreme enlightenment.
Whether walking or standing,
sitting or lying down,
having stilled discursive thought,
Delighting in the stilling of thoughts,
such a bhikkhu is capable of touching the supreme enlightenment.
This matter too was spoken by the Blessed One; thus have I heard.
The eleventh [discourse].
